summary.text: A 70-year-old married Caucasian Norwegian woman was referred to outpatient psychological treatment after being diagnosed with PTSD and recurring depressive episodes. Her history included childhood emotional abuse and neglect, childhood sexual abuse, her brother’s death, a suicide attempt at age 17 and a suicide attempt at age 17 and a sleeping pill overdose at age 18, her husband’s affair and divorce, her ex-husband’s death, and an accident at age 50 that severed her upper spine.

At age 65 her health deteriorated with intrusive memories, anxiety, depressed mood, nightmares, headaches, back and neck pain and social isolation. After a neurologist assessment she had psychiatric assessment and stabilizing inpatient treatment with psychoeducation, but symptoms continued and she was referred to outpatient trauma-focused psychotherapy. At intake she had hyperarousal, anxiety, dissociation, severe nightmares, disturbed sleep, fatigue and reduced social functioning, while taking antidepressants prescribed for decades.

Having chosen narrative exposure therapy over other options, she had four rapport sessions, then 11 sessions of NET including psychoeducation, a lifeline exercise and nine narrative exposure sessions, ending with re-reading of the written narrative, plus a booster session one month later. Symptoms were assessed at baseline, during treatment, after treatment and at follow-up.

At baseline all clinical symptoms were in the clinically significant range. At post-treatment PTSD symptoms were near mild levels and depressive and anxiety symptoms were in the mild range, with no adverse events. At follow-up the gains in PTSD and depressive symptoms were maintained, while anxiety symptoms returned to moderate levels.
